01

Should your first ice trip use a guide or a rental house?

Start by deciding which parts you want someone else to handle. A rental house can reduce the equipment you need, but a house booking alone does not tell you how much instruction you get. Ask for the service details in writing before you choose.[1]

Swipe the table to compare all columns.

OptionUseful whenAsk before booking
Guided sessionYou want help with tackle, depth, and bitesWill the guide stay with you, or check in at intervals?
Heated day-house rentalYou want shelter without an overnight stayAre rods, bait, transport, and help included?
Sleeper-house rentalYou want an overnight tripWhat bedding, water, toilet, ventilation, and emergency contact arrangements apply?
Trip with an experienced friendYou can borrow the large equipmentWho checks the route, brings rescue gear, and decides when to leave?
Choose a short first outing

Leave room to change the plan if someone gets cold, the access changes, or the fishing does not hold their interest. A shorter session also makes it easier to learn one setup before adding more gear.

02

How do you check the route before you fish?

Start with a lake you know and an experienced local ice angler. Check recent conditions, access restrictions, and the forecast.

Inspect and measure the ice as you travel; one hole does not describe the whole route. Stay away from current, inlets, outlets, pressure ridges, and aerated water.

Snow can hide weak areas. Tracks and other anglers are not proof that your route will support you.

Carry accessible ice picks, a throw rope, and a charged phone protected from water. Wear suitable flotation for travel on foot.

Tell someone the location and return time, and go with a partner. Keep a clear way back to shore.

If the ice changes underfoot or the weather threatens that route, leave. Treat local thickness guidance as a minimum condition to assess, never as a promise of safety.[2]

04

Where should you start looking below the ice?

Use a depth map to choose a weed edge, a point, or a break into deeper water. Pick a manageable area on the checked route.

Drill a few holes across the change in depth, then keep the loose ice clear. Measure the depth at each hole with your lure or a sounder.

Note where the weeds end and the bottom drops.

For panfish, start near remaining vegetation or a nearby deeper edge. Search above the bottom as well as close to it; fish can suspend.

A sonar unit helps show fish and your jig, but careful depth changes still teach you without one. Give each hole a fair try, then move within the assessed area if nothing happens.

Keep a productive hole quiet. Repeated drilling beside another angler can disturb both the fish and the day.[1] [3]

05

How do you work a jig for panfish?

A short rod, light line, and a small jig make a useful panfish setup. Add a tiny soft plastic or a permitted piece of bait.

Lower it to the chosen depth, then use small lifts and pauses. Watch the line and rod tip.

Some bites pull down; others remove weight as a fish lifts the jig. Raise the lure slowly if a fish follows but stops short.

For walleye or larger trout, use a jigging spoon or other lure sized to the target. Avoid one heavy, constant pumping motion.

Try a lift, a fall under control, and a pause. Where tip-ups are legal, set an allowed bait at a measured depth and attend the gear closely.

Check local line and hook limits before setting more holes. Keep spare rigs ready so cold fingers spend less time tying knots.[3]

06

How do you stay warm in and outside a shelter?

Wear dry layers and waterproof insulated boots. Carry spare gloves because bait, slush, and fish quickly wet the first pair.

Open layers before hard work, then close them when you stop. A small pad under your feet can make a stationary session more comfortable.

Keep warm drinks and food accessible, and shorten the trip if anyone becomes cold or tired.

A shelter blocks wind, but heaters need proper ventilation and the manufacturer’s clearances. Use suitable carbon monoxide protection with fuel-burning equipment.

Keep the exit free of tackle and loose line. Early and late light can be productive, so organize the return before darkness hides the route.

Follow local rules for shelter removal and marking large holes. Remove bait, litter, and line when you leave.

Keep released fish out of freezing air as briefly as possible.[1] [1]

A few good questions

Before you head out

Do you need to buy an auger for your first ice trip?

Not if an operator or companion supplies one. Confirm who drills the holes and what happens if you need to move before you buy large equipment.

Does a heated fish house include a guide?

Do not assume it does. Ask whether someone stays with you, gives an initial lesson, or only checks in. Compare that answer separately from the house and transport.

Can one ice measurement prove that the whole lake is safe?

No. Ice varies across a lake and changes with conditions. Check the full route repeatedly and follow local access restrictions. Other tracks do not establish safety.

What boots should you pack for ice fishing?

Pack waterproof insulated boots suited to the conditions, with the socks you will actually wear. Carry dry spare socks. River waders do not replace appropriate flotation or rescue gear.

Do you need a Minnesota fishing licence in a rental house?

Check your own licence requirement and any stated exemption. A house rental does not itself establish a personal licence exemption. Check the official rules for the exact water and species.

Can a beginner catch panfish without sonar?

Yes, sonar is not required to try the method. Measure the depth, work a small jig at different levels, and watch the line. Sonar can help show fish and the lure, but it cannot promise a bite.

SHOPPING LIST

Ice fishing shopping list

  • Ice fishing rod and reel combo

    A short 24–32 in rod for jigging through a hole.

    Check price ↗

  • Ice jigs and spoons

    Small tungsten jigs for perch and panfish; spoons for walleye and trout.

    Check price ↗

  • Hand auger or auger blade

    Skip this if your guide drills the holes.

    Check price ↗

  • Ice picks

    Wear them around your neck every time you walk on ice.

    Check price ↗

  • Ice cleats

    Slip-on spikes for bare, slick ice.

    Check price ↗

  • Insulated waterproof boots

    Rated for -40 °F; you stand still for hours.

    Check price ↗

  • Bucket seat with tackle storage

    A seat, a tackle box and a fish bucket in one.

    Check price ↗

  • Skimmer scoop

    Keeps the hole clear of slush.

    Check price ↗

  • Hand and toe warmers

    Cheap and easy to keep in every pocket.
